newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: SOCCER-HAVELANGE BACKS ARGENTINA'S GRONDONA AS SUCCESSOR.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER-HAVELANGE BACKS ARGENTINA'S GRONDONA AS SUCCESSOR.

text.p: World soccer chief Joao Havelange has backed Argentine Julio Grondona, who has been in charge of his country's federation for nearly 20 years, as his potential heir.
The 80-year-old Brazilian, due to retire as FIFA president next year, declared open hostilities with Europe with his support for Grondona.

He also overlooked his own son-in-law Ricardo Teixeira, who has been president of the Brazilian Football Confederation (CBF) since 1989. The family connection had led to inevitable speculation that Teixeira was being groomed to take over from Havelange.
"Julio is a great friend, he's like my brother," Havelange told a news conference in Buenos Aires.
"He's a great leader who may continue along the road I took many years ago if he is elected president of FIFA.
"But before that we must fight, especially against European countries who want to place their candidates at the helm of world football."
Grondona has been president of the Argentine Football Federation (AFA), a post considered more important than most government ministries, since 1979.
Although blighted by hooliganism, the Argentine game is one of the best organised in Latin America.
Grondona has been re-elected several times and has worked under both the military regime and democratically-elected governments of varying political inclinations.
The owner of a small business on the outskirts of Buenos Aires, Grondona became prominent as president of the Independiente club.
Grondona is a FIFA vice-president. He was appointed last December as chairman of FIFA's finance committee but has never shown any interest in the FIFA presidency.
He was the man who, as head of the Argentine association, had the task of announcing at the 1994 World Cup in the United States that team captain Diego Maradona had failed a dope test.
Teixeira's Brazil produces world-class players in spite of the organisation of its national game, which is chaotic, with crippling fixture lists and bizarre competitions nobody really understands.

The CBF was recently struck by a match-fixing scandal and although Teixeira himself was not incriminated, he was widely criticised for his handling of the affair. Consequently, few eyebrows were raised in Brazil at Havelange's announcement.

"Although it is an international success, Brazilian football is not an example of good administration," newspaper columnist Roberto Benevides said. "I think that Havelange is aware that his successor could never be a Brazilian."

UEFA head Lennart Johansson of Sweden is the leading candidate to replace Havelange, while FIFA's Swiss general secretary Sepp Blatter has also been tipped as a possible successor. Non-European names mentioned include Issa Hayatou of Cameroon.

Havelange has made it quite clear in the past that he does not want Johansson to get the job and soccer insiders say there is a growing body within FIFA concerned about possible future "Europeanisation".
One top non-European FIFA official has reportedly written to Havelange asking him to delay his retirement and stand again at the election in 1998.
But Havelange seems set on leaving the position he has held since 1974, although he had previously refrained from naming his preferred heir.

"I don't think we have ever heard this before, that he would support any particular individual," said UEFA spokesman Frits Ahlstrom of Havelange's ringing endorsement of his old South American friend.
Johannsson was on holiday and not immediately available for comment.
Soccer sources have said in the past that now Havelange has declared his retirement, he has lost much of his power in influencing FIFA decisions.
"I think UEFA's attitude in this would be that we never show surprise or disappointment because we don't expect anything," Ahlstrom said.
However, he did say that he thought it "only natural" for Havelange to back Grondona as an old friend and rejected the assertion that the battle lines were drawn.
"That would be against the attitude of Mr Johansson," he said. "He wants to see FIFA as a family like UEFA.
"He never sees it as a battle between Europe and the rest of the world. We never talk of a battle. We prefer to talk of dialogue and discussion."
FIFA spokesman Andreas Herren said that the world body's general attitude was one of no comment.
